newsitem.title: FRANCE: Snecma narrows 96 net loss 280 mln Ffr, sees gain.
newsitem.headline: Snecma narrows 96 net loss 280 mln Ffr, sees gain.

text.p: French state-owned aerospace group Snecma narrowed its loss for 1996 and forecast a net profit for the current year, citing a pick-up in civil aviation which should continue into 1998.

Snecma, which makes civil and military aero-engines and bought out the rocket motor maker Societe Europeene de Propulsion (SEP) last year, reported a 1996 group net loss of 280 million francs ($49.2 million) compared to 853 million in 1995.
Operating profit climbed to 444 million from 260 million, on turnover of 18.7 billion francs, up four percent.
It said a positive trend in civil aviation orders and restructuring efforts led it to forecast a 500 million franc net profit for 1997.
"The favourable trend in orders in civil aerospace allows us to expect a 20 percent increase in turnover for 1997 which should continue in 1998," it said in a results statement.
"The combination of recovery in activity and continuing restructuring efforts should lead to significantly positive results for the current year (500 million francs)," it said.
A reorganisation in the second half of 1996 into three areas -- propulsion, mechanical equipment and services -- was aimed at giving Snecma the best chances in the market, it said.
That policy continued in the first quarter, with its aerospace brakes activity being placed under the management of SEP, which makes the motors for the Ariane space rockets.
Snecma delivered 438 CFM56 aero-engines last year and motors for launching 10 Ariane 4 rockets. Some 75 percent of the turnover was in civil markets and 60 percent went in exports.

Snecma has been badly hit in recent years by a drop in civil aircraft orders and declining defence spending. But with a strong recovery which began last year in the world passenger aircraft market, it is benefiting from new orders.
It makes the CFM56 family of civilian engines in the CFM International joint venture with U.S. General Electric Co , which are sold on Boeing and Airbus aircraft.
